prompt: Capacitance is C = Q over V, the charge stored per {{1}} applied.
explanation: Per volt. It is a ratio, and crucially a FIXED one: raise the voltage and you push in proportionally more charge, so Q/V does not move. Capacitance is set by geometry, never by what you store in it.

prompt: The capacitance of an isolated sphere is C = 4 π ε₀ R, so a larger sphere has a larger capacitance.
explanation: True. R is the only variable in it, so capacitance rises directly with radius. Notice what is absent: no Q and no V, because they cancelled when C = Q/V was formed. That cancellation is the clearest proof in the course that capacitance depends on geometry alone.

why.true: Correct. R on top, so bigger sphere means bigger capacitance.
why.false: Wrong. R appears in the numerator, so growing the sphere grows the capacitance.

topic: what changes a parallel plate capacitor
prompt: For C = εᵣ ε₀ A over d, which change INCREASES the capacitance?
explanation: d is in the denominator, so a smaller gap gives a bigger capacitance. That is why real capacitors use very thin insulating layers. Area helps too, since A is on top, and so does a dielectric, since εᵣ is at least 1. Voltage does nothing at all: it is not in the formula.

why.c: Wrong. A is on top, so less area means less capacitance.
why.d: Wrong. Vacuum has εᵣ = 1, the smallest possible, so this reduces it.
why.e: Wrong, and it is the classic misconception: no V appears in the formula at all.

prompt: Capacitors in parallel add directly, C = C1 + C2, which is backwards from how resistors behave in parallel.
explanation: True. Capacitors add in PARALLEL and combine reciprocally in series; resistors do exactly the opposite. Physically, putting capacitors side by side is just building one larger plate, so the capacitances sum. The reliable way to remember is to learn one of the four cases properly and flip it for the other.

why.true: Correct, and the flip is the safest way to keep the pair apart.
why.false: Wrong. It is series capacitors that combine reciprocally.

prompt: Capacitance is defined as the charge stored per volt applied, and is measured in farads.
explanation: True, and the farad is a coulomb per volt. It is an enormous unit in practice: the capacitors in this course run from pF to μF, and a 1 F capacitor would be a remarkable object. Seeing an answer of 4.77 F should therefore fail the step 7 believability check instantly.

why.true: Correct on the definition and the unit.
why.false: Wrong. C = Q/V is precisely the definition, and F = C/V follows from it.

prompt: A dipole is two equal and {{1}} charges separated by a small distance.
explanation: Opposite. A polarised atom is the everyday case: an applied field pulls the electron cloud one way and the nucleus the other, producing exactly this arrangement. Its dipole moment is p = qd, pointing from the negative charge to the positive one.

A coulomb per volt, read straight off C = Q/V. The other four options are all real units of other things, which is why they make good distractors: a coulomb per second is the AMPERE, a joule per coulomb is the VOLT, and a volt per amp is the OHM.

why.a: Correct. A coulomb per volt, read straight off the definition C = Q/V.

prompt: Permittivity, symbol ε, describes how readily a material permits an electric field, while permeability, symbol μ, describes how readily it permits a {{1}} field.
explanation: A magnetic field. The two names are deliberately parallel and so are their roles: ε₀ appears in every electrostatic formula, μ₀ in every magnetic one. Their product is what gives the speed of light, which is how the two subjects turned out to be one.
